A detection model with its range shifted, for misspecification tests

perturb_de_model.Rd

Returns a copy of a detection model whose curve reaches 0.5 at d50_scale times the original 50 percent distance and 0.05 at d05_scale times the original 5 percent distance, and whose overdispersion standard deviations are multiplied by sigma_scale. Simulating detections with one model and positioning them with a perturbed copy shows what a wrong range model does to the positions.

Usage

perturb_de_model(model, d50_scale = 1, d05_scale = 1, sigma_scale = 1)

Arguments

model

A de_model from detfield::de_model() or detfield::de_logistic().

d50_scale

Factor for the distance at which half of the transmissions are detected; above 0.

d05_scale

Factor for the distance at which 5 percent are detected; above 0. With unequal scales the scaled 5 percent distance must stay beyond the scaled 50 percent distance. This is checked when the model is made, at the curve's default conditions; a curve that needs a depth or a transmitter model to be read is checked at each condition when it is asked.

sigma_scale

Factor for sigma$station_hour and sigma$station_day; 0 or more. A standard deviation that is NA stays NA.

Value

A de_model with the same modulators, blocked offset and transmitter models as model, a new predict function, the scaled sigma, and a source line that names the scales. The scales are also stored in the attribute perturbation.

Details

The new curve reads the original one at a warped distance. With equal scales the warp is a plain rescaling, distance / scale, which is exact for any curve: every distance at which the curve takes a given value is multiplied by the scale. With unequal scales the warp is the straight line through the two anchor points, so a curve that is linear in distance on the logit scale, such as detfield::de_logistic() or a logistic glm on distance, stays logistic: perturb_de_model(de_logistic(250, 600), 0.5) predicts what de_logistic(125, 600) predicts. The anchors are found by bisection for each combination of depth, transmitter model and modulators the curve is asked about. Near the receiver the line can give a negative distance; a logistic curve or a glm extends its slope there, and a table of curve values holds its first value.

See also

evaluate_array(), which takes a perturbed model as control$position_model.

Examples

m <- detfield::de_logistic(d50 = 250, d05 = 600)
short <- perturb_de_model(m, d50_scale = 0.5)
short
#> <de_model> perturb_de_model(d50 x 0.5, d05 x 1, sigma x 1) of:
#>   de_logistic, d50 250 m, d05 600 m
#>   reads: distance_m 
#>   sigma: station_hour not given
#>   blocked line of sight: curve read at the distance through water
plogis(short$predict(c(125, 600)))
#> [1] 0.50 0.05

# Twice the range everywhere, and twice the per-hour spread.
m_sd <- detfield::de_model(m, sigma = list(station_hour = 1))
long <- perturb_de_model(m_sd, d50_scale = 2, d05_scale = 2, sigma_scale = 2)
long$sigma$station_hour
#> [1] 2
plogis(long$predict(c(500, 1200)))
#> [1] 0.50 0.05

# Score the 20 planned stations when animals are detected under the true
# curve and positioned with one whose 50 and 5 percent distances are half
# of it. The depth raster is averaged to 200 m cells to keep the example
# short.
stoney <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "stoney_depth.tif",
                                  package = "arraydesign"))
stoney_200 <- terra::aggregate(stoney, 2, na.rm = TRUE)
planned <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "planned_stations.csv",
                                package = "arraydesign"))
rx <- place_receivers(stoney_200, method = "manual", coords = planned)
range_model <- detfield::de_logistic(d50 = c(250, 750), d05 = c(500, 1500),
                                     depth = c(1, 35))
short <- perturb_de_model(range_model, d50_scale = 0.5, d05_scale = 0.5)
ev_short <- evaluate_array(rx, stoney_200, range_model, n_animals = 20, seed = 1,
                           control = list(hours = 6, tag_delay = c(120, 180),
                                          position_model = short))
ev_short$score$overall[c("median_error_mean_m", "hit_rate")]
#>   median_error_mean_m hit_rate
#> 1            443.5522 0.140026
